strengths: The proposed detector addresses a practically relevant gap: scoring text in a single pass against fixed human/machine references, avoiding both classifier retraining and per-input regeneration. The compute/throughput analysis (Figure 6) is a useful and concrete deployment-oriented contribution.

The theoretical analysis is more complete than is typical for this area: the paper identifies the GJS gap with a normalized log-likelihood ratio (Proposition 4.3), derives an explicit bias-variance trade-off yielding k* = Θ(N^{1/5}), and proves asymptotic normality of the decision statistic by adapting second-order expansion techniques (Zhou et al. 2018) and CLTs for additive functionals of Markov chains (Holzmann 2005).

The experimental coverage is broad: 12 source models, 5 datasets, ablations over bins/reference length/test length/proxy model, non-English evaluation, paraphrase robustness, and a comparison with the closely related R-Detect.
The empirical validation of asymptotic normality (Figures 2c, 7) is a nice touch connecting theory to practice.
weaknesses: The 'black-box / unknown source model' framing is weakened by the experimental design: machine reference corpora are generated by prompting the *same source model* being tested. The theory itself assumes the test source MT is exactly MP or MQ. There is no systematic study of detection when the machine reference comes from a different model than the test text's true source, which is the core claim of the setting. This mismatch between claimed setting and evaluated setting is the most serious conceptual issue.

Test sets are very small (150 human + 150 machine texts per dataset) and the generation protocol is narrow (prompting with the first 30 tokens of a human text, no varied decoding parameters, no adversarial prompts, no human-rewritten or mixed human-machine text). Evaluation on a broad stress-test benchmark (RAID/DetectRL) appears only for the R-Detect comparison.

There are apparent arithmetic errors in the main Table 1: the LogRank average is reported as 46.53 while its three components (53.87, 66.8, 49.83) average to 56.83; DetectLRR's average (62.11) does not match its components (44.51, 63.29, 49.83 → 52.54) either. Errors in the primary results table undermine confidence in the reporting.

A theory-practice gap in the discretization analysis: Proposition 4.1 asserts the existence of a shared k-bin partition achieving O(1/k) error, but the method uses k-means on pooled reference surprisals, and no result shows that the k-means partition satisfies the required conditions (e.g., the mean-radius/O(1/k) argument in Eq. 85 depends on quantizer properties that are not established for k-means under the actual surprisal distribution). The claim that k=6-7 is 'near-optimal' from k* = Θ(N^{1/5}) involves hand-waving about an unspecified constant C.

The main asymptotic normality result (Theorem 4.4) is stated 'informally' and relies on assumptions (ergodic first-order Markov surprisal sequences, bounded mixing time, π_min ≳ 1/k) whose validity for real proxy-LM surprisal processes is asserted rather than verified; the Markov assumption is supported only empirically via a heat map (Figure 2b) on one dataset.

No explicit limitations section; robustness is evaluated only against T5 paraphrasing on three dataset-model pairs, and there is no analysis of false-positive behavior on out-of-domain human text, which is the practically critical failure mode for reference-based detectors.

Reproducibility is thin: the statement amounts to 'All experimental projects in this paper are reproducible' with a pointer to the appendix; no code release is mentioned, and several implementation details (threshold τ selection, zero-count corrections, k-means fitting procedure) are not fully specified.

Originality is moderate: the method combines known ingredients (surprisal quantization from Lastde, first-order Markov modeling, GJS, Gutman's two-reference testing), and the relative-test framing is shared with Song et al. (2025). The contribution is a coherent synthesis with supporting theory rather than a fundamentally new idea.

strengths: Clear practical motivation: SurpMark scores each text in a single pass with no per-instance regeneration, contrasting with costly distributional methods (DetectGPT, Fast-DetectGPT, DNA-GPT), and the reference-budget analysis (B=2 vs. B=10–10000) makes the efficiency claim concrete.

Substantive theoretical contribution: the paper establishes (i) a non-asymptotic discretization-statistical error decomposition for Markov sources extending Pillutla et al. (2023) from IID to Markov chains, yielding a principled k* = Θ(N^{1/5}) bin choice, (ii) an exact identification of ΔGJSn with the normalized log-likelihood ratio (Prop. 4.3), and (iii) asymptotic normality of the decision statistic under ergodicity (Thm 4.4). Proofs are detailed and appropriately leverage Markov concentration tools (Wolfer 2023, Skorski 2020, Chung et al. 2012, Holzmann 2005).

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: 12 source models (including GPT-5-Chat and GPT-4.1-mini), 5+ datasets, non-English (Chinese, German) scenarios, paraphrase-attack robustness (Table 9), throughput analysis, and extensive ablations (bins k, reference size, test/reference length trade-off, proxy model choice) with standard deviations over repeated runs.
Theory is connected to practice: the predicted optimal k is checked against empirical optima (Figures 3–4), and score distributions empirically corroborate the Gaussian limit (Figures 2c, 7).
Honest positioning relative to R-Detect: the paper acknowledges shared 'relative test' foundations and includes a direct comparison (Table 10), plus a discussion of trade-offs in computational cost.
Ethics and LLM-usage statements are present and appropriate; implementation details are provided and the reproducibility statement indicates code/data availability.
weaknesses: Tension between the 'black-box, unknown source model' framing and the experimental protocol: the machine reference corpus is generated by prompting the *true source model* (including closed-source ones via API). In real deployments the generator is unknown, so the required machine reference is unavailable; the proxy-mismatch ablation varies only the scoring proxy, not the machine reference. This materially limits the reach of the central black-box claim.

Arithmetic inconsistencies in the main tables undermine confidence: e.g., in Table 1 the LogRank average is reported as 46.53 but the three per-model values (53.87, 66.8, 49.83) average to ~56.8, and DetectLRR's average (62.11) does not match its entries (44.51, 63.29, 49.83). Similar mismatches appear elsewhere (e.g., Table 2 vs. Tables 6–8 averages). These need correction and explanation.

The evaluation setting (30-token-prompted continuations from the same corpora used for references) is a relatively benign detection scenario; robustness is assessed only via a T5 paraphrase attack on three configurations. Stronger adversarial evaluations (e.g., RAID's adversarial subsets more broadly, mixed human/AI documents, iterative human editing) would strengthen the deployment claims.

The threshold τ in Eq. (2) is described as 'tunable' but the paper does not specify how it would be set in practice. Given the asymptotic normality result, a calibration/p-value procedure or false-positive-rate analysis at fixed thresholds would be a natural and expected use of the theory, but this is not provided.

Theoretical assumptions are strong relative to practice: first-order Markov structure of discretized surprisals, TV-Lipschitz transition kernels (Assumption A2.4), and πmin ≳ 1/k. The paper provides only indirect empirical support (Figure 2b for model order); the gap between assumptions and real text statistics is not quantified.

Novelty is incremental relative to recent work: the relative-test framing overlaps with R-Detect (Song et al. 2025) and discretized probability-sequence features with Lastde (Xu et al. 2025); the main new elements are the Markov-transition summary and the GJS/LLR identification. This is a useful but not groundbreaking combination.

Presentation issues: several typos and grammatical errors ('These motivates', 'an lightweight', 'The proof are relegated', 'exits' for 'exists'), the k=6 vs. k=7 variant reporting in Table 1/2 is ad hoc, and the derivation for the k* constant factor is loose (the text itself concedes N^{1/5}≈9 while recommending k=6–7).

strengths: Extensive and well-designed empirical evaluation: 12 source models (including frontier closed-source systems such as GPT-5-Chat and GPT-4.1-mini), 8 datasets, 13 baselines, and multiple stress-test scenarios (mixed-domain, mixed-generator, domain-shift OOD, cross-source corruption, paraphrase attacks, decoding-strategy variation, non-English corpora, Kaggle DAIGT mixed-generator benchmark). The consistency of gains, especially the strong margins on closed-source models (Table 3, Table 12-14), makes the empirical claims convincing.

The paper develops genuine theoretical support for the design rather than hand-waving: a discretization-estimation tradeoff (Prop. 3.1 + Thm. 3.2) yielding k* = Θ(N^{1/5}), an exact identity between ΔGJS and the generalized log-likelihood ratio (Prop. 3.4, extending Gutman's LFHT to a two-reference setting), and asymptotic normality (Thm. D.14). These are empirically probed (Table 18 bin-count calibration, Table 19-20 variance/normality checks), which is more than typical for this area.

Good experimental hygiene: human-machine pairs are length-matched, decoding configurations are disclosed, results are averaged over multiple random test sets with standard deviations, TPR at low FPR is reported (Table 21), and the theoretical/explanatory analyses (marginal vs. transition surprisal gap in E.2.12, pretraining-exposure confound in E.2.18) address likely alternative explanations for the results.

Honest treatment of limitations and ethics: the paper clearly scopes the Markov approximation as an idealization of the proxy-scored discretized states (not the generative process), discusses pretraining-exposure artifacts, and includes a responsible impact statement warning against sole reliance on the detector for high-stakes decisions.

The efficiency argument is well quantified: single-pass scoring with a one-time reference build gives a 5x-50x lower reference budget and favorable throughput (Figure 6), a practically meaningful advantage over perturbation-based detectors.
weaknesses: There is a gap between the theory and the deployed method. Theorem 3.2/Prop. 3.1 assume idealized first-order Markov kernels on continuous surprisal space with Lipschitz conditional TV (Assumption D.4), ergodicity, π_min ≳ 1/k, and, importantly, the discretization-error bound (Prop. 3.1) holds only for a specially constructed partition ('there exists a shared k-bin partition'), whereas the method uses k-means binning. The constants are also loose: the empirical k/N^{1/5} ratio ranges 0.71-0.88 (Table 18, described as 'consistently around 0.8'), and theoretical variances deviate from empirical ones by factors of 2-9x (Table 19). The theory thus justifies qualitative trends (moderate k, first-order sufficiency) rather than precise design, which the paper mostly acknowledges but could state more carefully.

The first-order Markov justification relies on a proxy model (GPT-5-chat and its human counterpart only in Table 11, with Î ≈ 0.0076 bits/token); it is unclear this negligible second-order dependence holds broadly across proxy models and generators, so 'first-order sufficiency' may be dataset/proxy-specific.

Originality is moderate: the components (discretized token-probability features, as in Lastde/Lastde++; reference-based relative testing, as in R-Detect; Jensen-Shannon-type divergences; Markov modeling of score trajectories) are each established; the contribution is a novel and reasonably principled combination plus new analysis rather than a fundamentally new mechanism. Baselines are also somewhat uneven in some settings (e.g., R-Detect performs poorly in Table 2 despite being a close relative, warranting more discussion of tuning fairness).

Minor presentation issues: several typos ('decoding stratigy', 'threhold', 'Genmma', 'are stationary distributions'), and the claimed 'ranks first on 6 of 9 / top two on 7 of 9' counting in Section 4.1 should be stated against explicit best-in-column criteria; some tables (e.g., Table 2 vs. its per-dataset expansions) make the best-per-column verification tedious.
No explicit statement that code will be released; reproducibility rests on the detailed configuration descriptions and public datasets/known baselines, which is adequate but could be strengthened.

Effect sizes on some datasets are modest for open-source sources (e.g., SQuAD, Table 14/17, where SurpMark is sometimes behind Lastde++ or Fast-DetectGPT per-column), so 'consistently matches or surpasses baselines' is somewhat stronger than the per-dataset evidence.

strengths: The paper is unusually comprehensive in its empirical evaluation: 12 source models (including recent closed-source ones like GPT-5-Chat and Gemini-1.5-Flash), 8 datasets, comparisons against 13 baselines, and a large set of ablations covering decoding strategies, paraphrase and adversarial attacks, mixed-domain/mixed-generator settings, proxy-model sensitivity, and OOD references.

There is a genuine attempt to connect the design to theory: the two-reference GJS statistic is shown to be a generalized log-likelihood ratio extending Gutman's LFHT (Prop. 3.4), a discretization–estimation tradeoff motivates k = Θ(N^{1/5}) (Thm. 3.2), and asymptotic normality is derived and empirically checked (Shapiro–Wilk tests, variance comparison).

The method is practical and well-motivated: single-pass scoring without per-input regeneration, one-time reference construction, and low compute cost, with a throughput analysis quantifying the break-even point against Fast-DetectGPT.
The analysis in Appendix E.2.12 (marginal vs. transition divergence ratio explaining why closed-source models are hard for marginal-statistic detectors) is an insightful empirical contribution.
The limitations section and impact statement are honest and specific, including the pretraining-exposure confound, which the authors directly test in Appendix E.2.18.
weaknesses: Limited originality. The core recipe—discretize proxy-LM token probabilities, model the resulting sequence, and compare against human/machine references—closely parallels existing work: Lastde++ already discretizes token probabilities for entropy features, R-Detect performs exactly the human-vs-machine anchor comparison, and FourierGPT/Lastde exploit token-probability trajectory structure. The 'recovery phenomenon' motivating the feature is also not new. The delta over these works is mostly the specific statistic (transition-matrix GJS), which feels incremental for a main-track paper.

Overclaiming relative to the evidence. The claim that SurpMark 'consistently matches or surpasses baselines' is contradicted by the authors' own tables: on closed-source models it is second to Binoculars on Gemini@WritingPrompts (Table 13), behind Lastde++ on XSum@Gemini (Table 12), and behind several baselines on individual open-source cells (e.g., Lastde++ on SQuAD@GPT2-XL, Table 17). The advantage is largely on averages, not uniformly.

Numerical inconsistencies undermine confidence in reporting. In Table 3, the Avg column does not match the per-model values for LogRank (reported 46.53 vs. computed 56.83) and DetectLRR (reported 62.11 vs. computed 52.54). Similar spot-checks elsewhere should be re-verified.

Experimental setup concerns. (i) The machine reference corpus must be generated by the (unknown) source model for the main benchmark, which arguably weakens the 'black-box, unknown source' framing—this is only partially addressed via the mixed-generator and cross-reference studies. (ii) The paraphrase-OOD experiment (Table 9) paraphrases the very texts in the reference sets, so near-perfect AUROC (99+) may reflect content overlap between reference and test rather than robust paraphrase invariance; this leakage is not discussed.

Gap between theory and practice. Proposition 3.1 is an existence result over partitions, whereas the method uses k-means; Theorem 3.2 assumes ergodicity, bounded mixing time, and π_min ≳ 1/k, which are strong idealizations not verified for real text. The theory mainly provides post-hoc rationalization of a tuning choice (k), with the constant C ≈ 0.8 calibrated empirically after the fact.

Reproducibility is not assured: no code release is stated; implementation is described only as 'adapted from MAUVE and Lastde.' Combined with the reporting inconsistencies, results would be difficult to verify as-is.

Some writing issues (e.g., 'strategiy', 'Genmma', 'threhold', inconsistent theorem numbering 'Theorem D.3.3') and dense appendix derivations that, while substantial, mostly re-package known tools (Wolfer, Pillutla, Holzmann).
